hints: Think about what is controlling the speed at the very start compared to later on, when product and reactant amounts have changed.
At time zero there is no product yet, so there is no catalyst present and the initial rate must be zero or very low.
Combine the speed-up from making more catalyst with the slow-down from using up reactants to picture how the rate first rises and then falls.
walkthrough:
**Think about the start of the reaction**

At time = 0, only reactants are present. Because the catalyst is a product, its concentration is zero, so the reaction starts very slowly.

This means the curve must start at the origin: $$\text{rate at } t=0 \approx 0$$

**Think about the middle speed-up**

As a little product forms, that product acts as a catalyst. More catalyst lowers the activation energy for more molecules, so the rate increases rapidly.

This gives the rising part of the curve, the reaction speeds itself up.

**Think about the end slow-down**

Later, even though lots of catalyst is present, the reactants are running out. With low reactant concentration, collisions become rare and the rate must fall again toward zero.

Rise then fall gives a peaked curve starting at zero, which matches the autocatalytic shape.

options.A: Incorrect. This curve starts fast from zero and then stays at a high constant rate. In a real reaction the rate cannot stay high forever because reactants are consumed.
options.B: Incorrect. This shows a slow start and speed-up, which is correct for autocatalysis, but then it levels off and stays high. It forgets that falling reactant concentration will eventually make the rate decrease.
options.C: Correct. Rate starts at zero (no catalyst yet), rises to a maximum as product catalyst builds up, then falls as reactants are used up. This rise-and-fall peaked shape is characteristic of autocatalysis.
options.D: Incorrect. This is the normal rate against time curve for an uncatalysed reaction, fastest at the start when reactant concentration is highest. It is the opposite of autocatalysis, where the start is slowest.
